speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is significantly higher than the global average of 69%.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is very low compared to other major cities, such as Sydney, London and New York.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To ensure that Singaporeans continue to enjoy high levels of safety and security, we should ensure that our crime fighting capabilities are cutting edge, and that Police have access to useful tools to detect and solve crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In 2002, a 12-year-old schoolgirl was raped but the identity of the suspect could not be established at the time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Twelve years later in 2014, a man was arrested for alleged theft and a blood sample was collected from him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Through the DNA profiling of his blood sample, Police discovered that his DNA profile matched the one found at the rape crime scene in 2002.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The rapist was charged and sentenced to 16.5 years' imprisonment and 18 strokes of the cane.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This Bill, therefore, seeks to enhance the Police's capabilities to solve crime, using DNA evidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In the course of Police investigations, the Police may collect samples at the crime scene.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These crime scene samples will be analysed to obtain DNA profiles which will be compared against profiles in the Police's DNA database.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We should expand the Police's DNA database to bolster their ability to solve crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fingerprints and DNA are unique to an individual, except for identical twins who share the same DNA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fingerprint matching and DNA profiling can help the Police identify and place a particular individual at the crime scene or exonerate the individual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fingerprint matching suffers at times from the inability to lift a complete fingerprint at the crime scene.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: DNA profiling, on the other hand, is not limited to one source as DNA information may be derived from minute amounts of body samples such as saliva, sweat or blood droplets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: DNA profiling is thus a useful and well-established forensic tool, and is widely used by law enforcement agencies worldwide to solve crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: According to the INTERPOL Global DNA Profiling Survey, about 70% of the member countries which responded to the survey reported using DNA profiling in police investigations and at least 70 countries have a DNA database.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The United Kingdom started to use DNA profiling in criminal investigations in the 1980s and established a national DNA database in 1995.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Apart from the rape case in 2002, several cases, including cold cases, have been solved, both locally and overseas, through DNA profiling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For instance, between 1986 and 1991, 10 women were killed in Hwaseong, Korea.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Almost 30 years later in 2019, through DNA analysis of crime scene samples, police eventually identified the real killer and the innocent man was exonerated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: DNA profiling is an effective tool to help the Police solve crimes, by identifying possible suspects accurately and quickly, and exonerating the innocent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But the effectiveness of this forensic tool in criminal investigations depends, in large part, on the size of the Police's DNA database.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A larger database means a higher chance of obtaining a match.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Conversely, a smaller pool of DNA data would be less effective in helping the Police solve crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If we want our laws to be enforced effectively and to continue to enjoy a high level of safety and security in our daily lives, our law enforcement agencies must be provided with as many forensic tools as reasonably possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We may have Police cameras in many public places today, but they do not cover the scenes of all crimes, for example, if they take place in homes or other private areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Similarly, other forensic tools which the Police already have, may be able to help solve some but not all the crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I will now describe the amendments we are looking to make, to enhance the effectiveness of DNA profiling as a tool to help the Police solve crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This Bill amends the Registration of Criminals Act 1949 in the following ways: (a) expand the scope for the collection of DNA information and other identifying information; (b) expand the prescribed uses of DNA information; (c) strengthen the protection of DNA information; and (d) introduce procedures to allow the removal of information in the databases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, on expanding the scope of collection of DNA information and other identifying information. "DNA information" is defined in the Act to refer to genetic information derived from the forensic DNA analysis of a body sample. "Identifying information" will be defined to refer to other information that can help identify an individual, including fingerprints, photographs and descriptions of the individual such as sex and age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will expand the scope of crimes eligible for the collection of DNA information and identifying information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 6 repeals and re-enacts part 3 of the Act to provide for the collection of DNA information and identifying information from individuals involved in two categories of offences: registrable crimes and eligible crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Registrable crimes are crimes that are currently included in the First or Second Schedule to the Registration of Criminals Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These are usually more serious crimes, such as murder, rape and robbery.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: An individual who is convicted of a registrable crime will have a criminal record.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, Police can only take fingerprints and body samples from an individual who is accused of, convicted of, or imprisoned for a registrable crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If we had been able to collect DNA and identifying information from these individuals when they were convicted of a non-registrable crime, we might have been able to identify them a lot more swiftly, when they later re-offended and committed the registrable crime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Other countries collect DNA information for a far broader scope of offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, South Australia collects DNA information for all imprisonable offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will be defined as an "eligible crime" and will be inserted into the Act by clause 2(d) of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Eligible crimes are, therefore, the more serious crimes, and will not include minor offences such as littering and illegal parking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Individuals who commit eligible crimes may have their DNA information and fingerprints taken, but will continue to not have any criminal record as such crimes are not registrable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Examples of eligible crimes include voluntarily causing hurt and affray.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will not collect DNA information and fingerprints from individuals involved in minor offences, such as littering and illegal parking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will also expand the scope of collection for persons dealt with under the Internal Security Act 1960 (ISA).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, we can only collect fingerprints from individuals who are arrested or detained under the ISA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We also cannot collect DNA information and fingerprints of those who are not arrested and are only served with a restriction order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 6 will insert new sections 13 and 22 to allow the collection of DNA information and identifying information from individuals who are arrested, detained or served with a restriction order, under the ISA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In England, South Australia and the Netherlands, any individual can voluntarily provide his body samples for forensic DNA analysis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 6 will insert new sections 14 and 23 to allow any individual to voluntarily provide his DNA information and identifying information to the Police to assist in investigations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 6 will also insert new sections 37 and 38 to specify that volunteers who have provided their information, may apply to the Police to remove their information from the databases at any time and the Police must do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will also make it clear that it is an offence for an individual who refuses, without reasonable excuse, to provide a body sample and introduce a new offence for a parent or guardian of an individual below 16 years of age to withhold consent, without reasonable excuse, for an invasive sample to be taken from the individual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To complement these expanded powers for the collection of DNA information, we will make it clear that any person who unreasonably refuses to provide a body sample, including a blood sample, commits an offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Generally, a person provides his DNA information through providing a body sample, such as buccal sample or hair sample, or a blood sample.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Blood samples are generally preferred to other samples, as they are more likely to yield a high quality DNA profile, that can be reliably used to obtain a valid DNA match downstream.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: More than 99% of the body samples that are taken today are blood samples.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Before taking a blood sample, a DNA officer must ensure that the taking of the blood sample does not endanger the individual and the DNA officer will obtain the consent of the individual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Thereafter, the officer will prick the individual's fingertip to obtain a small sample of blood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If the individual has a reasonable excuse to refuse the taking of his blood sample, for example, he suffers from a blood disorder such as haemophilia, the Police will not take his blood sample and will take other body samples from him instead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If he refuses to provide a blood sample, he may be taken before a Magistrate, who may order him to provide the sample.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A negative inference may also be drawn against him in court, in criminal proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The amended Bill will no longer require the individual to be brought before a Magistrate before he may be liable for an offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The new section 27 will make it clear that a person who refuses without reasonable excuse to provide a body sample, including a blood sample, commits an offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will also make it an offence for a parent or guardian of an individual under 16 years of age to withhold consent, without reasonable excuse, for an invasive sample to be taken from that individual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, DNA information stored in the DNA database may be used for a few purposes: (a) forensic comparison with any other DNA information in the course of Police investigations into an offence; (b) comparison with DNA information in the DNA database established under other Acts; (c) proceedings for any offence; and (d) administering the DNA database.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They are: (a) investigation or inquiry into a death; (b) identifying a dead individual; and (c) identifying an individual in order to provide Police assistance to the individual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Before the information is shared, the foreign law enforcement agency will be required to undertake to safekeep the information, limit the use of the information to the specified purpose and comply with other conditions imposed by the Police.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will legislate safeguards to protect the DNA information and identifying information stored in the databases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Access to the DNA database will be restricted to authorised officers, every access to the database will be recorded and we will provide for an audit trail.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 12 will amend section 14A, which will be renumbered to section 49 by clause 9, to empower the Minister to make rules to introduce safeguards that the Registrar must implement to protect the information recorded in the databases against any loss, modification, or unauthorised access.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Where investigations reveal that a suspect is not involved in the commission of the crime, or where the suspect was arrested and detained under the ISA and investigations subsequently reveal that he had not acted in a manner prejudicial to the security of Singapore, his DNA information and fingerprints will continue to be automatically removed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Individuals who are acquitted or given a discharge amounting to an acquittal by the Court and individuals who have their offences compounded, can apply to the Registrar for their information to be removed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Upon the individual's application, the Registrar will remove all DNA information and identifying information of the individual from the databases, unless it is relevant for any ongoing prosecution or investigation, or it is in the interests of the security of Singapore to retain the information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Any person who disagrees with the decision of the Registrar may appeal to a Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The above is provided for in the new Part 6, which introduces procedures to allow individuals to apply to the Registrar to remove their registrable particulars, identifying information and DNA information from the databases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This new Part 7 provides for the establishment of Reviewing Tribunals and for appeals against the Registrar's determination to be made to the Tribunal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The application and appeal process is straightforward and simple.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The individual may apply to the Registrar of Criminals to request for his information to be removed from the databases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Within 30 days of the application, the Registrar determines whether any of the following two grounds exist.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: One, the applicant's information is relevant to another ongoing prosecution or investigation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Or two, retaining the applicant's information is in the interests of the security of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If none of these grounds exist, the Registrar will remove the applicant's information from the databases and notify the applicant that his application is successful, and that the information has been removed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If any of the grounds exists, the Registrar will notify the applicant that his application is unsuccessful.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Registrar will state the ground for the rejection and the applicant may decide if he wishes to appeal to the Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If the applicant wishes to appeal to the Tribunal, he must do so within 30 days from the date of the notice of the Registrar's determination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Reviewing Tribunal comprises a District Judge or Magistrate, who is appointed by the President on the advice of the Cabinet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Reviewing Tribunal can either confirm or revoke the decision appealed against.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, the Tribunal must dismiss an appeal if the Registrar presents a certificate issued by the Minister, certifying that the applicant's information was taken in relation to an offence under the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act 2021 or the Internal Security Act, and that it is in the interests of the security of Singapore to retain his information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: (In Mandarin):   In the course of Police investigations, the Police may collect samples at the crime scene.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These crime scene samples will be analysed to obtain DNA profiles which will be compared against profiles in the Police's DNA database.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: DNA profiling is an effective tool to help the Police solve crimes, by identifying possible suspects accurately and quickly, and exonerating the innocent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But the effectiveness of this forensic tool in criminal investigations depends, in large part, on the size of the Police’s DNA database.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A larger database means a higher chance of obtaining a match.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: (In English): In sum, the proposed amendments to the Registration of Criminals Act will enable law enforcement agencies to carry out their duties more effectively, to ensure the safety and security of Singapore, while balancing those expanded powers against individuals' right to privacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, I have concerns about the Bill and will seek clarifications later in my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In scrutinising the Bill, the Workers' Party reviewed the situation in other jurisdictions to better understand how DNA information is collected and utilised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In South Australia, for example, the offences covered under the Criminal Law Forensics Procedures Act 2007 includes all offences punishable by imprisonment, not dissimilar to our position but technically broader than the position taken in today's Bill, which excludes some offences punishable by imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the United Kingdom, under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act, blood and other intimate samples, or what this Bill refers to as invasive samples, can only be taken with written consent without exception.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a position that is less intrusive upon the rights of the individual than the one proposed by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, non-intimate samples, which includes hair and swabs that would allow the collection of DNA, can be taken in the UK without consent if the person is under investigation for what is called a recordable offence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This appears to be a broader position than the one proposed under this Bill, as the meaning of a recordable offence is very wide and it may include offences not punishable by imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Japan, there is no specific statute governing from whom and under what circumstances DNA may be collected.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the Japanese authorities have adopted an approach to DNA collection that is one of the most aggressive in the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By late 2019, the police in Japan had collected close to 1.3 million DNA samples, which covers about one in 100 of the Japanese population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Data released under Japanese information disclosure laws in late 2019 showed that those alleged to have committed serious crimes, such as murder, burglary and rape, accounted for only 4.8% of the DNA database.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By contrast, DNA was collected for 210,000 persons suspected of violating the Road Traffic Law, the Swords and Firearm Law, the Immigration Control Law and the Minor Offence Law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This accounted for about 16% of the entire database.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I should add that every DNA sample was collected only after the suspects gave consent to register their DNA information in the national police agency database.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our review of other jurisdictions shows that there is no consensus as to the boundaries and ambit of DNA collection.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But we can certainly pick out some useful points.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For Singapore, we need to ensure that our Bill suits our circumstances and protects our citizens.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, Sir, I seek four specific clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will list them and then elaborate on each of them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, the proposed section 32(h) allows any information in the DNA database to be used for such purposes as may be prescribed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister clarify whether the Government intends or foresees the use of DNA information for purposes other than for Police investigations into specific cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And if not, will the Government undertake to return to this House to seek Parliamentary approval if the DNA database is to be used for non-investigation related purposes?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, could the Minister clarify what factors authorised officers would take into account in deciding whether to take DNA samples from those convicted of eligible crimes?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, could the Minister tell us the cost of taking a DNA sample of an accused person or convicted individual.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: DNA data is not akin to non-DNA identifying information like fingerprints.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, it is possible to use DNA information to create a profile of an individual by comparing their DNA data to a larger DNA sample size.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This cannot be achieved with an existing register of fingerprints.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our DNA can tell a story or highlight predispositions that most people would not know about themselves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, certain versions of a gene on the X chromosome that codes for monoamine oxidase enzyme (MAO) are associated with sensation-seeking and impulsive tendencies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another example is the Per2 Gene which has been linked with advanced sleep phase syndrome that informs which individual is more predisposed to going to bed early and rising early, while Per3 is found in night owls.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Both these data points taken to the extreme can indicate the likelihood of possible criminal tendencies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this era of big data, artificial intelligence and machine learning, the purposes for which the DNA information is collected becomes exceedingly important, something Parliament must scrupulously guard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Seen in this context, the Bill envisages the surrender of private information for which the highest levels of security and access must be assured by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just a few years ago, in 2018, the personal information of some 1.5 million Singaporeans was hacked in the SingHealth cybersecurity breach, the worst publicly known cybersecurity incident in Singapore's history.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Officers who misuse their powers will be dealt with severely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With reference to the proposed section 49(1A), can the Minister confirm if the DNA database would be stored in a standalone computer or in systems that are linked to the Internet and therefore susceptible to cyber-attack?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How wide is the access to the DNA database?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What was the range of punishments that have been meted out to such officers?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And what recovery procedures and remedies can citizens whose DNA information has been compromised or used in a way not sanctioned by legislation avail themselves to?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second clarification is on the further uses of the DNA database.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With such depth of personal information extractable from DNA data, Parliament should be apprised of the limits on the use of such data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This greatly expands the use of DNA information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I invite the Minister to clarify what other uses of DNA information are being contemplated under paragraph 32(h)?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, and this is certainly not exhaustive, it is not beyond imagination that this clause could be relied on to use the DNA database for purposes of profiling and to draw inferences about groups of people as being a relatively greater public order threat compared to others, as alluded to earlier.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If there is no such intention, can the Minister clarify the ambit of paragraph (h) for the record?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It must be the Government's position that it would return to this House should the DNA database be used for any other purpose other than Police investigation into specific cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister confirm this to be so?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister clarify what is the thinking behind not mandating the taking of DNA information but instead giving an option to the authorised officer?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is especially relevant since the public statements of the Ministry in justifying this Bill – I beg your pardon – in tabling this Bill have thus far alluded to expanding the DNA database.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What are the types of cases or scenarios this Bill conceives of where the authorised officer would need to decide for or against the taking of DNA information from an individual and what is the basis of those decisions?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What consistency will be applied for the purposes of the proposed section 10 vis-a-vis eligible crimes?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourth and finally, Mr Speaker, as is routine in every Bill that comes before this House, the explanatory note contains a section titled "Expenditure of Public Money".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is understandable because, for example, the exact number of DNA samples to be collected and processed for eligible crimes cannot be known at this time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, it should be possible to know the cost of taking individual samples, if not a broad estimate based on crime statistics over the last five to 10 years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim will speak on other matters for the Minister's clarification.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would add that the hon Member for Holland-Bukit Timah Mr Christopher de Souza, who is away on State duty today and therefore unable to speak on this Bill, has expressed to me his strong support for the Bill too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He is of the view that this Bill enhances the ability of enforcement agencies to act swiftly to identify suspects of a broader array of crime accurately and apprehend them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek clarification on three areas from the hon Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, it is proposed that the current section 13G of the Act, which deals with removal of identifying information or DNA information from the register upon acquittal or discharge be repealed and be substituted with the proposed section 37(3) and 37(4) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the proposed section 39(1) in the Bill, the Registrar must remove the same unless he is of the view that the information is relevant to an ongoing prosecution or investigation or it is in the interest of national security.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note from the Hansard that the hon Minister for Home Affairs then, Mr Wong Kan Seng, in moving the amendment Bill in 2002 to set up the DNA database and elaborating on the kind of information that will be retained, stated as follows, "What happens to body samples of persons acquitted or discharged?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, the Act requires the Registrar of Criminals to destroy the photograph and finger impression of a person acquitted or discharged within three months from the date of acquittal or discharge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Similarly, clause 5 requires the Registrar to remove the DNA information of a person from the DNA database within three months of his acquittal or discharge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Is it necessitated by a change in the law and order situation?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Why is not preferable for the current mechanism of automatic removal be maintained?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The proposed system appears to benefit those with the resources, the time and the know-how to request such a deletion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for the hon Minister of State's clarification.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to clauses 24 and 28 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These clauses combined provide that where an accused refuses to provide his consent for the taking of a sample to determine whether or not he has committed an eligible or registrable crime, the Court may draw an inference from the refusal that the Court thinks proper.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The accused will also be liable for an offence of failing to given a sample without reasonable excuse under clause 27.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The approach taken in this Bill brings to my memory the salutary approach adopted in section 23 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Section 23 deals with the recording of a cautioned statement from a witness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The accused must be served with a written notice that he has to state his defence in his statement, failing which the Court may draw an adverse inference against him for not doing so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In that sense, warning becomes a lot more important under the current paradigm as opposed to what was proposed in 2002.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that the provisions in the Internal Security Act dealing with the taking of body samples is proposed to be ported over to the Registration of Criminals Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, the enhanced safeguards will apply to body samples collected from ISA detainees.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As it stands, the provisions dealing with the collection of samples continue to be dealt with by the same provisions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under section 27C of the CLTPA, it is provided that the Commissioner of Police shall cause to be maintained both a register and DNA database for persons arrested or detained under CLTPA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Similarly, under section 40D of the MDA, the Commissioner of Police must again maintain both a register and DNA database for drug addicts who are subject to supervision or are in drug rehabilitation centres.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the face of it, it does not appear that the added safeguards are being proposed to be enacted in the CLTPA and MDA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am also unclear why there should be separate registers and DNA databases in other pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would have thought it would be more synergistic to consolidate all the registers and databases under one piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for the hon Minister of State's response.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: No one can quarrel with the Ministry’s aspiration to strengthen the crime investigation capabilities of the Police for the security of our nation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, in the pursuit of enhancing Police capability in crime solving, there are three key needs that are important to address.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Even if giving up one’s personal data is the consequence of committing a crime, the state should not over-infringe the bounds of a citizen’s privacy rights.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I feel the Ministry should explain how this additional list of offences is decided upon.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What were the factors of consideration when the Ministry decides on which offences are included?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, would even a first-time offender of, say, dangerous driving, be compelled to have his DNA collected?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Advancement in technology means higher risks of hacking and of information being compromised.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not unimaginable that much more can be done with DNA data, such as creating fake profiles, digital identity stealing, cloning and the like.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Personal data, when fallen into wrong hands, can lead to dire consequences.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Given that so much more sensitive personal data is collected by the state, what are the additional safeguards to ensure that the database, especially of DNA information, is better protected?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What is the accountability of the agency should such personal data be leaked or compromised, whether locally or internationally?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will potential volunteers who might come forward to offer their DNA information to the Police be better briefed so that they can better make informed decisions before volunteering?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is unclear how the vulnerable are protected in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For the vulnerable, it is not so clear from the Bill that the Police have a positive duty to inform the individuals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that the vulnerable will not be at a disadvantage, compared to those who are more able and knowledgeable?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I refer especially to individuals who are above 16 years of age and who lack the mental capacity to fully understand the implication of what they say or agree to.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of those with special needs and disabilities will need a familiar figure to explain and guide them during interrogation, the collection of blood sample and through the rest of the process.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the early phases of the COVID-19 pandemic, there was an outcry on how the needs of residents with special needs were not accommodated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It took much education and convincing of the authorities to change the Government’s vaccination, quarantine and safe management processes to make the needed accommodations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And then there are individuals who may not be lacking in mental capacity but are less educated and less tech-savvy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Take, for instance, the Bill’s introduction of tighter procedures for the removal of personal data collected in the Criminal Records Office’s database.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But unless properly advised and assisted, the less-educated and less tech-savvy individuals may not know how to exercise this right to apply to remove their DNA information nor how to make an application even if they know.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But I seek clarification on what I feel are important needs to protect individual privacy, personal data collected and to protect especially the vulnerable.
