speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The first case happened in 1979 when four children of the Tan family were murdered in their flat in Geylang Bahru.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There was no evidence of forced entry nor was their house ransacked.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although bloodstains were found in the kitchen sink, DNA technology was not advanced enough then to identify the culprit and the murders remain unsolved today.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Subsequently, in 1981, a temple medium, Adrian Lim, together with his two partners, murdered two young children, aged nine and 10 then, at their flat in Toa Payoh.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The murderers were apprehended only after they had killed the second child.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was when CID inspectors traced the bloodstains at the crime scene to the staircase steps leading to the floor of the same block, near to Adrian Lim’s flat unit.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was the infamous Toa Payoh ritual murders.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What if these cases can be solved by identifying the criminals through the DNA databases owned by our Singapore Police Force?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened to know that the advancement of forensic medicine has greatly improved the possibility of apprehending criminals in recent years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: DNA identifying information has become useful tools for crime-solving.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the high success rate in solving murders through DNA information in recent years, enabling a larger database for our Police Force to compare the samples from crime scenes can help tremendously in our criminal investigations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The amendment Bill is thus a timely response to increase our Police Force’s capabilities to solve crimes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, like the collection of any other information that is personal, there are ethical and privacy considerations that we need to contend with.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, I would like to raise clarifications in two main aspects: one, the collection of DNA identifying information for eligible crimes under the amendments; and, two, the storage of the information collected.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, under section 9 and 18(1) of the amendment Bill, an authorised officer may collect the DNA and non-DNA information from the individual accused of an eligible crime.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under section 64 of the Road Traffic Act 1961 (RTA), the sentencing of reckless or dangerous driving causing hurt is considered based on the injury caused to the victims, depending on four levels: death, grievous hurt, hurt and minimal or no injury.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under RTA, the sentencing framework of (a) hurt and (b) minimal or no injury, does not carry a mandatory imprisonment sentence and the offence appears to be compoundable under section 135 of RTA .

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My concern is for individuals who are accused or convicted of driving without due care or reasonable consideration – which section 65 of RTA states as “any person who drives a motor vehicle on a road (a) without due care and attention; or (b) without reasonable consideration for other persons using the road”.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From time to time, I have attended to residents who have been charged in Court under section 65 of RTA during my Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most of them committed the offence unintentionally and were remorseful of their actions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In other words, it is not a deliberate act of harm.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, in the amendment Bill, it did not explicitly state the requirements for special needs individuals, whom I consider as vulnerable even if they are above 16 years of age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I share the same concerns as hon Member Ms Denise Phua.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, section 25 re-enacts with modifications section 13E(5)(b) which empowers a DNA officer to use reasonable force to take a body sample.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In relation to my point on special needs individuals, despite being accused individuals, I believe that they are to be considered vulnerable adults and may warrant special attention to their needs and emotions while they undergo the potentially traumatic experience of being an accused person.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thirdly, new sections 29 and 32 will be inserted into the amendment Bill to provide for the maintenance of an identifiable database that stores the records of DNA and non-DNA information of individuals accused and convicted of an eligible or registrable crime.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It also laid out that the purpose on which the DNA database may be used for investigation into a death, identifying a dead individual or for identifying an individual to provide Police assistance.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The compromised data included certain personal and medical information.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such news shows the risk of network security breaches and the safeguards that need to be in place.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   As forensic analysis capabilities and technologies improve, personal information such as DNA, fingerprints and photographs have become the key for solving crimes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I believe that by including those who have committed eligible non-registrable crimes in the scope of data collection through the Registration of Criminals (Amendment) Bill, the database will be expanded to provide a more effective tool for the Police to solve crimes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I hope that MHA will clarify that when collecting invasive samples of juvenile offenders under the age of 16, the written consent of the person, parent or guardian will be sought based on the needs of different age groups.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel that people with special needs and the intellectually disabled, even if they are over the age of 16, are still vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, there is a need to have provisions to give special attention to them, especially to their mental state, and to protect their rights and interests.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Where necessary, provide appropriate assistance when collecting samples from them to help them, their parents, and guardians to understand the procedures and cooperate with the DNA officers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, back to English, please.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Forensic medicine advancement has contributed to more effective criminal investigations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To our investigators and forensic pathologists, the pieces of evidence that they collect, including DNA data in a secured database, can lend a voice to the victims who suffer the brutality of the crimes committed against them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the family and friends of the victims in murder cases, it offers the opportunity to bring closure to the death of their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Being a nine-year-old schoolmate of the first murdered child in the Toa Payoh ritual murders, I can speak personally of the trauma I felt when I heard the tragedy about 40 years ago and the closure I had when the murderers were finally brought to justice.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There is no doubt that DNA evidence and identification have helped solve numerous crime cases in and around the world and have been a boon for law enforcement agencies in cracking many major, violent, serious and organised crimes and have led to the successful arrest, prosecution and conviction of highly dangerous and wanted criminals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Notwithstanding, I wish to submit that there should be adequate safeguards in three important areas: DNA collection, DNA use and DNA disclosure.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have five questions and clarifications for each of these three areas for MHA to respond to and clarify so that we are all properly and unequivocally apprised of the necessary safeguards as we embark on this DNA journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One, there are numerous ways to collect DNA and I hope MHA can enlighten us on the ways and methods in which the DNA will be collected, or maybe there might only be one method, so that we can better understand how invasive the process may potentially be.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Two, will young, youthful, intellectually-disabled, aged and other vulnerable persons also be subjected to this DNA collection process?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And as we know, some young offenders can still be in Primary school and I am concerned that the process may be traumatising to a young offender.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Four, what safeguards will there be in place to prevent contamination of DNA in the entire collection and examination process?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Five, whether this collection and examination will be outsourced to private organisations outside of the Singapore Police Force.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One, I note that DNA collection will be for registrable offences.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Two, can MHA also share how the actual DNA sample as well as the information and data of the DNA sample will be stored?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Three, once stored, how is it protected and safeguarded, so that it shall not be illegally accessed and leaked whether by physical, cyber or virtual means?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Four, for how long will the sample and the data on the sample be stored?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One, can MHA also share how and who this DNA data will be shared with and disclosed to during investigations, prosecution and also in a Court trial as part of the criminal discovery process?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Three, will the DNA information collected also be shared with agencies outside of SPF, such as CPIB, CNB, ICA, MOM, MAS, CRA or even other agencies with quasi-enforcement and quasi-investigation powers, including with private organisations, such as insurance companies, when they investigate insurance fraud or corporate fraud and so on?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Four, the other parts of the Act have provisions for offences to be "spent".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Will it, therefore, follow that DNA samples will be spent when offences are being "spent"?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Five, how will the DNA sample and data be managed in the eventuality of a disposal of the case?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such information helps law enforcement agencies to do their work more effectively.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Because such information is sensitive, I support provisions in the Bill that protect such information when it is collected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have four clarifications, all relating to the safeguards for the collection and removal of this information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification has to do with the forcible taking of samples.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I think we can all agree that having a body sample forcibly taken from us can be intrusive, distressing and traumatic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how will DNA officers be trained to decide whether they should use force to take a body sample?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What factors will DNA officers be asked to consider?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be checks and penalties to ensure that such acts of force, once done, are warranted and justified?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the taking of samples from those below 16 years of age.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should exercise extreme caution when taking samples from such young people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is well-established that children and younger teenagers lack the ability to understand the full implications of their bodily consent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They do not know what they are really saying yes to, and there is good reason that the consent of parents and guardians is routinely required in such decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this Bill allows DNA officers to, essentially, ignore the parents and guardians' preferences under certain conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first condition is that the consent of the parent or guardian is refused without good cause or cannot be obtained despite reasonable efforts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State provide examples of what would constitute good cause and reasonable efforts?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second condition is that the underage person is "willing" to give the sample.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify how DNA officers will ensure this "willingness" is an informed, meaningful one?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that the child or young teenager in this situation may feel pressured by the Police or other powerful adults bearing down on them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What rules and checks will be in place to ensure DNA officers, Police officers and other officers do not create undue pressure on these young minds to consent?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third clarification is on the removal of recorded information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The onus is on them to apply to remove their data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share how these individuals will be informed of the option to apply for their data to be removed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What steps will be taken to ensure that the application process is transparent and reasonably easy to access?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Relatedly, it seems that an individual granted a discharge not amounting to an acquittal may not apply for their information to be removed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify if this is, in fact, the position?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that a discharge not amounting to an acquittal is significantly different in nature from a conviction, can the Minister of State share if discretion may be exercised to allow the removal of information if there is a discharge not amounting to an acquittal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State also clarify whether an individual who has been given a stern warning will have their data information immediately removed after the end of investigations or will be entitled to apply for such removal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My last clarification has to do with the application process to remove information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 39 makes clear that certain individuals will be rejected if they apply to remove their information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is because their information is considered sensitive, it is relevant to another ongoing prosecution or investigation, or there are other national security concerns.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My question is this: will these individuals be told when their information is no longer considered sensitive?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, how will they know whether they should apply again or not?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just as important, how will prescribed timelines apply to such individuals?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How can they be expected to follow the prescribed timelines for a removal application when their information may be sensitive for a long time and then become non-sensitive without their knowledge?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, the individual had already demonstrated their preference for the removal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should not require someone to apply again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If these individuals will be required to reapply, will they be informed of the opportunity to make a fresh application?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, Madam, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Amongst other capabilities, investigation plays a key role in solving crimes and upholding public confidence.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We must continue to support our officers with the right investigation capabilities and legal framework, so that they remain effective in keeping Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On this basis, I believe the amendments in this Bill on the collection, use and storage of information from case persons are well-intentioned and sound.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Nonetheless, I would like to seek some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While this will boost timeliness of collection, as a safeguard, can the Minister of State share if this process will be authorised and supervised by an officer who is appropriately trained and qualified?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Greater assurance could, for example, be achieved by requiring officers of a minimum rank, similar to the requirement stated in the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I ask this as the clause appears to be counter-intuitive since volunteers, who have a weaker connection to a case compared to suspects, are required to apply to the Police for removal of their data under clause 37(2).

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I note that clause 32 sets out the usage of DNA information for limited purposes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding, can the Minister of State explain what are "other purposes" under clause 32(h) that may be prescribed?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill also proposes the sharing of DNA results of convicted criminals with foreign LEAs when assessed necessary.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This expands the current regime where registrable information, such as fingerprints, are already shared.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As a safeguard, the foreign LEA will need to provide an undertaking to safekeep the data, limit its uses and destroy it upon conclusion.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Also, considering varying levels of cybersecurity infrastructure across jurisdictions, as well as difficulties of monitoring foreign LEAs, can the Minister of State share how compliance with the undertaking by foreign counterparts will be ensured?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill also introduces a new category of "eligible crimes", expanding the current scope of crimes eligible for information to be collected.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Per clause 2(d) of the Bill, these are defined as any offence punishable with imprisonment, except those compoundable.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: With the foreseeable increase in the size and sensitivity of data collected, retained and used, I am encouraged that the Bill will also legislate safeguards for the handling of information, such as having persons accessing the databases to be screened and authorised by the Police.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It follows that with greater powers come greater responsibilities to further strengthen trust in our LEAs.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Some of our agencies have, unfortunately, been impacted by data leakage due to cybersecurity attacks.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Going forward, the world is seeing more cybersecurity threats which are also becoming increasingly sophisticated.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, as we continue to build our capabilities, we must be wary that what has happened can occur again.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: DNA samples, I understand, are collected on blotter cards, but the data analysed are stored on computer databases, which can be subject to the cybersecurity threats I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Without being overly technical, will measures recommended by our Public Sector Data Security Review Committee, such as digital watermarking, encryption, tokenisation and multi-party authorisation, be deployed or further enhanced to strengthen cybersecurity?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Through the use of data, our LEAs must send the message to potential criminals that they will be caught.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: But it is also critical that we must balance the expanded collection, retention and usage of personal information with safeguards in data privacy and security.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, public trust amongst our LEAs can be upheld.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am confident that this Bill will enable our officers to continue keeping Singapore safe and secure and I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill, amongst other amendments, aims to enhance the collection of information from suspects which will provide the authorities with a larger database to compare samples from crime scenes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A larger database would simply mean that cases may be solved more effectively and efficiently.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Police have been using DNA to help solve crimes from 1991 and the ability to extract DNA from a crime scene and run it through a database has greatly improved the odds of Police in solving cases.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, DNA profiling was crucial in solving a case of a serial fatal stabbing in 2010.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In that case, the absence of CCTV footage, fingerprints as well as DNA had hindered Police from getting leads.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, at the fourth occurrence, the blade of a knife had broken off and it was found some metres away from the deceased.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Police then found a plastic sheath that was used to cover the knife, where they were able to extract DNA samples, develop a profile and identify the perpetrator.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will allow volunteers the confidence to step-up and provide them with the opportunity to protect exonerate themselves.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A relative may come across as a partial match.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There are also instances where there are doppelgangers, people who look strikingly similar, but are not related.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thirdly, with evolving technology, there have been many advancements, amongst them, DNA fabrication.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How does the Police safeguards against this and what are the plans by the Police to leverage on advancements in technology in DNA matching?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Upon collection of data and data storage, what safeguards are in place to protect the data: prevent the loss, modification and unauthorised access to any information recorded in various databases and also, would there be alternative secure storage locations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And, if so, will it be outsourced to an external agency?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   The Bill aims to enhance the collection of information from crime suspects through the comparison of DNA samples from a crime scene, with a larger database.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Police have been using DNA to help solve crimes since 1991 and the ability to use DNA analysis has greatly improved the chances of the police to solve cases.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A larger database would mean that cases may be solved more effectively and efficiently.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: More importantly, although DNA analysis can be used as evidence against someone, it can also be used to exonerate someone and prove their innocence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As such, I hope that the Minister can provide clarification about the steps that will be taken to safeguard and protect the DNA data to prevent any modification and misuse.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, in conclusion, I am convinced that the expansion of the collection and the use of DNA data would enhance the Police's effectiveness and efficiency in solving crimes and exonerate the innocent, and hence make Singapore an even safer and more secure home.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: While we acknowledge that an expanded database would prove useful for criminal investigations, we must strike the correct balance between the need to collect and record samples while also protecting the rights and privacy of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How invasive are we going to be when collecting samples and what are procedures set in place to ensure that the collection and storage of samples does not infringe on the rights of our citizens?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Hence, while I agree with the Bill in-principle as our law enforcement officers should be given every tool possible to help with investigations, I would also like to make certain clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: The first point of clarification is whether this Bill will make the collection of DNA compulsory or admissible.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: In other words, will the Police take DNA samples in cases like "registrable" and "eligible" offences or the Police can, but need not always take a DNA sample?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: In a case of unlawful stalking, for example, which will be an "eligible" crime, where the stalker is already known to the victim, would the stalker's DNA still need to be collected at any point of the investigations?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How will the DNA sample be extracted then from such an individual?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: In a situation where there are multiple suspects for a single crime, for example, would all the suspects of such "eligible" crime have their DNA sample taken?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Does this apply to those currently serving term for "eligible" crimes?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: If the intent is to "grow" the database, it is more helpful in this case for the Police to collect as many DNA samples as possible as it is quite plausible that the DNA information would be useful, if not for the immediate case, it could still be useful in future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: However, we also do not want a situation where we indiscriminately collect samples from suspects.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: There should be proper criteria or procedure to follow to ascertain whether a sample needs to be taken or not.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: This is to ensure that we can maintain the privacy and dignity of suspects too while investigations are taking place.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Does it apply for suspects who are discharged not amounting to acquittal?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: It has to be reiterated that the collection of samples is to expand the database in order to help with investigations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: On what basis do we decide that a person's DNA sample or information would not be stored?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Would this inadvertently lead to delays in the administration of justice especially if there is a backlog created due to the inefficient collection and analysis of DNA data?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Perhaps, a breakdown of "registered" and "eligible" crime would be useful to make an informed projection of the number of samples expected.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Do we have sufficient professionals and trained personnel in the criminal justice system to ensure the optimal use of DNA as evidence to assist victims and solve crimes?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: It would be counter-productive if the collection of DNA samples as evidence leads to a delay in investigations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Lastly, how do we safeguard the data from being abused?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: How do we ensure that DNA data is safely secured from unauthorised access and protected from being modified or deleted?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: This should also extend to data that has been shared with foreign law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Under what contexts would it be necessary for our Police Force to share DNA information with foreign agencies, and how safe would the data be once it has been ported over?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Would there be safeguards against future use of this information beyond the original intent of this Bill?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: (In Malay):   This Bill intends to expand the DNA database and thus, enable the police to solve cases more effectively.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: However, I would like to seek the following clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: First, how will the DNA sample be extracted?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Do those currently serving time need to provide their DNA?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Second, for suspects acquitted of their crimes, discharged by the court, or found not to be involved in a crime, how much time is given to them to apply for their DNA information to be removed?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Third, do we have the capacity to process this new number of DNA samples arising from this Bill?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: Lastly, how do we safeguard this DNA data from being abused?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, notwithstanding the clarifications above, I am in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It enables investigators to expedite the identification of victims and suspects.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, its use will be efficient in assisting investigations if the data bank has the information of all residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more information and a bigger database, our Police's ability to solve cases and prevent crimes will be greatly enhanced.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, it is very important to ensure the data is safely protected against misuse, abuse and theft.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the protection of data is important, MHA should explore various options on how to ensure verification and certification instead of forwarding the data to a third party or foreign counterpart, if it is feasible.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must have a robust system for the collection of data.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important to prevent "garbage in, garbage out" and avoiding having the wrong samples collected or stored due to human error.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The risk of mismatches needs to be minimised or eliminated.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will expand the database, allow DNA information to play a greater role in helping the Police to solve crimes and to maintain public safety.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: DNA can also be used to identify the deceased persons and those who are unable to identify themselves.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are concerns about whether this DNA data can be kept safe from misuse.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we should not give up eating just because of the risk of choking.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Imagine someone who almost choked to death wants to forbid eating in the whole world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The analogy is that something which ought to be done is simply not done simply because of little fault or fear of a problem.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am confident that the authorities would do everything in their power to keep the information safe.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The medical book 千金药方 or "the Golden Rules of Prescription", says that the best type of medical treatment is to eradicate the root cause of the disease before it occurs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second best is treatment applied at the beginning of the disease and when the symptoms are superficial.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And third best is to give treatment only when the patient is in a critical condition and in extreme pain, and then help him to recover.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am sure everyone will agree that going to the first type of doctor is the best option.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, I have a few questions and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As a former Police officer with 20 years of working closely with frontline policing and investigation officers, I know first-hand how vital the collection of key identifying information, such as DNA and fingerprints, is for the purpose of solving crimes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In her Second Reading speech, the Minister of State had given us some examples of past cases that had been solved via DNA analysis.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Bill proposes to expand the prescribed uses of the DNA information collected.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I welcome this move as this will help our Police officers solve cases faster.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The amendments will not only allow DNA information to be used to identify a deceased person and for any investigations and inquiries into a death but will also allow for the identification of an individual who might be unable to identify himself and allow the Police to assist him.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How do we rank in terms of comprehensiveness of DNA and non-DNA data collection?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If there are other countries that allow the collection of DNA for a wider array of crimes, should we not follow suit?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I believe the Minister of State mentioned that South Australia collects DNA information for all imprisonable offences while England collects DNA information for imprisonable offences and some non-	imprisonable offences.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Why are we then limiting the tools that can help our Police officers obtain an investigation breakthrough and potentially solve a difficult crime?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition to the Bill's provisions to safeguard the data of DNA and non-DNA identifying information, we also need to ensure that the DNA samples themselves are subject to proper storage and disposal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In fact, why is there a need to keep the DNA sample once it has been processed, profiled and recorded?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond identifying criminals, a DNA registry can also be helpful in identifying missing victims or in an event with mass casualties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: From a victim's point-of-view, when he is in grave danger and in need of urgent help, every second counts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To the family of a victim in a homicide case, every possible tool to help bring the assailant to justice counts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To deter a potential criminal, increasing his risk of being caught counts.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There are five key stages in the collection and handling of DNA information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, a body sample is collected from the individual.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Second, DNA information is extracted from the body sample.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Third, the DNA information is stored in a secured database.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Next, the DNA information may be used for prescribed purposes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Sharael Taha asked how body samples are extracted from individuals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Typically, the DNA officer will obtain body samples in the form of blood.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I have explained that this is because blood samples are more likely to yield a high-quality DNA profile.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The DNA officer will sterilise the individual's fingertip, prick it with a disposable lancet and collect the blood droplets.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In situations where it is not feasible to collect a blood sample, the officer will do a buccal swab by using a sterile swab to swab the inside of the individual's cheeks on both sides.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, the chances of obtaining a high-quality DNA profile from buccal swabs are lower.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked whether the process of collecting blood samples will be authorised and supervised by officers of a minimum rank.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: All officers who take body samples will be trained.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There are standard protocols on the collection process.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Providing for further supervisors will take up additional resources, which we do not have.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether an accused who refuses to provide his consent for the taking of a sample would be issued a written notice warning him of the consequences of not doing so.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As part of the procedure to obtain consent, the accused will be asked to sign a form which will state the consequences of refusing to provide consent.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is no different from the practice today.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Denise Phua and Ms Ng Ling Ling sought clarification on whether certain traffic offences are eligible for DNA collection.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: To reiterate, DNA and identifying information can be collected for two categories of offences – registrable crimes, which are crimes currently included in the First and Second Schedule of RCA, and eligible crimes, which are non-registrable crimes punishable by imprisonment and not compoundable under any written law unless the offence is specified in the Fourth Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code 2010.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked whether the DNA collection provisions apply to persons who are currently serving sentences for eligible crimes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The new provisions apply to offences committed after the new law comes into effect.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked how officers may decide whether to take DNA samples.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Police will assess the nature of the crime, the evidence and whether to collect DNA information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On Mr Patrick Tay's question about the rationale for the expansion of the scope of collection of DNA information, the intent is to enhance the effectiveness of DNA profiling to help Police solve crimes.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked how the revised DNA collection regime would compare with that of other countries.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have surveyed the approach in foreign jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We did not just adopt wholesale the practices of other countries but, where appropriate, adapted them to suit our context.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have chosen to expand our collection only to offences that are punishable by imprisonment and not compoundable under any written law unless the offence is specified in the Fourth Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code 2010.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This strikes the appropriate balance in our local context.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Melvin Yong also suggested establishing a national DNA registry where the DNA sequence of every Singaporean and resident would be recorded.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Sharael Taha raised a concern about whether there are sufficient resources to deal with the increased load in collecting body samples.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Police will put in place the necessary infrastructure and resources to support the expected increase in load but it will mean that other areas will be even more stretched.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members also asked about the safeguards for the collection process.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Ng, Ms Ng Ling Ling, Ms Denise Phua and Mr Patrick Tay spoke about young individuals and individuals with special needs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Invasive body samples, such as blood samples, will only be collected based on consent.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If the individual is below 16 years old, the written consent of his parent or guardian has to be obtained.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how body samples may be taken from young persons and the checks that will be in place to ensure that such consent is given willingly.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, officers can take any invasive body samples for accused persons below 16 years old with the consent of their parent or guardian.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: However, non-invasive body samples, such as buccal swabs, can be taken without consent.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Second, where an individual below 16 years of age is a volunteer in the context of the Bill, officers may only take body samples, whether invasive or non-invasive, without his parent or guardian's consent when three requirements are satisfied.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: An example of a good cause can be when the volunteer suffers from blood disorders, such as haemophilia, and the taking of his blood sample may endanger him.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the rationale for imposing punishment on the parental guardian who does not give consent for body samples to be taken.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Parents and guardians are given the right to decide whether they will give consent on the behalf of their children.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If they withhold consent without reasonable excuse, it is their decision.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The question then should be why are they refusing if there is no reasonable excuse?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There should be an onus to give consent since Police are acting in the public interest.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked how we can protect vulnerable persons from being pressured to volunteer.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The law provides for voluntary giving of DNA.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: When people as adults make up their minds to step forward to volunteer, we should encourage it.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I think most people will accept that Singaporeans will make up their own minds.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As for foreign workers, the fact that they may be concerned about their work permits does not negate their consent.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They make their assessments and, if they have done nothing wrong, there is nothing to be worried about.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Denise Phua asked how volunteers will be briefed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As part of the procedure to obtain consent, volunteers will be informed that the DNA information provided will be used for purposes under RCA and that they have the option to request for their DNA information to be removed at any point.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the use of force to take a non-invasive body sample.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In deciding whether to use reasonable force, Police officers will assess the facts and circumstances of each case, including the urgency of the situation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If individuals feel that the force used was disproportionate, they can provide feedback to MHA or lodge a Police report.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The Ministry will investigate the complaint, and take action, where warranted.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: After the body samples are obtained, the individual’s DNA information will be extracted from the collected sample, profiled using genetic equipment and software, and the resultant DNA profile stored in the DNA database.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked if this process is outsourced to private organisations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: MHA engages the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) to administer the DNA Database Laboratory, generate DNA profiles from body samples taken under the RCA and upload them into the DNA database.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We do not engage private organisations to undertake this.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Dr Wan Rizal asked about the safeguards to prevent the contamination and mixing up of DNA profiles.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, the DNA sample that is collected is marked with a unique barcode number.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: After a person has given his body sample, it will be immediately sealed, in his presence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The barcode number will be recorded and the sealed sample is placed into a DNA collection box which will be locked, before being sent to the DNA Database Laboratory for forensic analysis.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The DNA profiles derived from both sets of duplicates are compared for any non-concordance and only the DNA profile of samples which produce identical profiles from the duplicates will be uploaded into the DNA database.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This duplication process eliminates potential errors in the uploading process, such as the wrong DNA profile being uploaded into the database.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Next, I will talk about the storage of the extracted DNA information and body samples.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Patrick Tay asked how the body samples and DNA information will be stored.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The body samples are stored in the DNA Database Laboratory at Police Cantonment Complex and the DNA information is stored in the DNA database which is hosted on a standalone secured network.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As for Mr Melvin Yong’s question on why we keep DNA samples after it has been profiled, Police keep the samples for two main reasons.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, to keep pace with technological developments – allowing us to re-profile the samples as technology advances to upkeep the quality of our records.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: And second, for quality assurance – so that if the information is challenged, it can be re-profiled from the sample.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members have asked questions about the data security measures and given suggestions to protect the sensitive information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Derrick Goh, Ms Ng Ling Ling, Mr Sharael Taha, Ms Denise Phua, Mr Patrick Tay and Dr Wan Rizal spoke about this.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There are practices in place to protect the DNA information and identifying information stored in the database.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Only authorised individuals are allowed to access the DNA database.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: All access is logged and recorded, through an audit trail, to detect any data modification.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The data is stored on a secured network to prevent unauthorised access.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There is also a framework in place to manage any Government data incidents.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In the event of a data breach, appropriate remedial actions will be taken in accordance with standard operating procedures and workflows.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We thank Mr Derrick Goh for his suggestion to strengthen cybersecurity measures.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We will continue to review and enhance the security of our systems.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked why the provisions dealing with the collection of body samples under other Acts were not consolidated under the RCA and about the safeguards for the databases maintained under the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act 1955 (CLTPA) and the Misuse of Drugs Act 1973 (MDA).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: There is no need to consolidate the provisions dealing with the collection of body samples under those other Acts in the RCA, as those Acts already have provisions dealing with the collection of body samples.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Next, I will talk about how the DNA information will be used.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked how the DNA information will be disclosed during prosecution.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: One example is where the DNA profile extracted from a crime scene sample is matched to DNA information in the database, leading to the identification of a possible suspect.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This can be tendered as evidence in Court.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and Dr Wan Rizal asked about the treatment of partial matches.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Generally, a partial match will unlikely be the sole piece of evidence that Police rely upon to identify the perpetrator.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Police use a range of investigative tools and leads to solve crime.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked if the DNA information collected can be shared with other agencies, private organisations or used for civil proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: As for sharing with foreign law enforcement agencies, which Mr Derrick Goh, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Patrick Tay spoke about, we will share particulars or DNA information of persons who have been convicted of a registrable crime for the purposes of foreign investigations or proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Further, the foreign law enforcement agency must comply with the conditions prescribed for the transmission of such information and any other conditions that the Singapore authority may impose.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Derrick Goh and Mr Sharael Taha asked about future uses of the information that may be prescribed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This relates to clause 13F(2)(d) of the current RCA.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The clause, for such other purposes as may be prescribed is not new.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is an existing provision under the current RCA.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This provision allows the Ministry to prescribe additional uses for DNA information via subsidiary legislation and such subsidiary legislation has to be published in the Gazette and presented to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Next, I will talk about the removal of information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Louis Ng, Ms Denise Phua and Mr Sharael Taha asked about the process to apply for the removal of information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The details of the application process will be made available on SPF’s website in due course.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether individuals would be told that their information is no longer sensitive so that they may re-apply to the Registrar to remove their information from the databases and how the prescribed timelines apply to these individuals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: When the Registrar rejects an individual’s application to remove his information from the database, the Registrar will notify the applicant and state the reasons for the rejection.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If his data has been retained because there is an ongoing prosecution or investigation, the individual should be aware when these are concluded, such that he may re-apply for expungement.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Where his data is retained due to national security concerns, we will not be able to inform him when these concerns no longer exist.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If he disagrees with the decision of the Registrar, he can appeal to the Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Even if the Reviewing Tribunal dismisses the appeal, the individual may re-apply for removal at any time.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Moving on to the removal of information from the database.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked why we require acquitted accused to apply for their information to be removed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The purpose of the database is to assist in crime-solving.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: When the acquitted accused applies to have his information removed, we will remove it except under two circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: First, where the information is relevant for another ongoing investigation or prosecution; and second, where it is in the interests of the security of Singapore to retain the individual’s data.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Subject to that, it is in society’s interests that there is a larger database of DNA – the DNA has to be collected and retained in acceptable ways.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If acquitted persons want their DNA to be removed, they can apply to do so.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked about the rationale for the default removal of the information of suspects who are found not to be involved in the commission of the crime, while volunteers need to apply for the removal of their information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Upon arrest, suspects would have been compelled to provide their DNA information, and failure to do so without reasonable excuse is an offence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, when we find out later that he is not involved in the crime, it would only be right that we remove his DNA information which we had acquired coercively.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the other hand, volunteers provide their information on a voluntary basis, and hence it is reasonable for their data to remain in the database until they apply to remove it.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: An individual granted a discharge not amounting to an acquittal has not been granted a full acquittal on the charge and the Public Prosecutor may still institute proceedings against the accused on the charge.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This may occur, for example, where an accused has absconded.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Thus, his information should not be removed from the database as it is still required for investigations or prosecution.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Persons who are warned are also not equivalent to persons who have been acquitted.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They were warned because investigations revealed that they were involved in the commission of the offence, but the Public Prosecutor has decided not to prosecute them in court.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked about the retention of information for individuals whose offences have been rendered spent.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Individuals who have their offences rendered spent are not equivalent to individuals who are acquitted or discharged.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The significance of a spent conviction is that the individual will no longer have a criminal record for the spent offence.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This facilitates his rehabilitation and re-integration, by removing stigma associated with a criminal record.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: His first question was on safeguarding the DNA database and access to it.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I had set out, in my Second Reading speech, what the safeguards are.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: All access is logged and recorded and there will be an audit trail to detect any data access.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The DNA information is stored on a standalone, secured network to prevent unauthorised access.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Singh wanted to know what will happen if an officer accesses information without authorisation under this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: When there is unauthorised access, action will be taken.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Members will be aware that in the past, officers have been charged in Court for unauthorised access or use of information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Most recently, Members may have seen media reports of two former prison officers who had been charged for unauthorised use of inmate information.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: One of the cases was in the news two days ago.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If any person feels that his information has been misused, he can lodge a complaint and the complaint will be investigated.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Action will be taken if the complaint is found to be substantiated.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Singh's second question relates to section 13F(2)(d) of the current RCA.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The provision for such other purposes as may be prescribed is not new.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is an existing provision under the current RCA.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This provision allows the Ministry to prescribe additional uses of DNA information via subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Such subsidiary legislation has to be published in the Gazette and presented to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Singh's third question is on how officers may decide whether to take DNA.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Officers on the ground will have to be given the discretion, exercise their judgement whether to take the DNA for the investigations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is not possible to prescribe precisely when they should and should not take DNA in future, because there are thousands of different situations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: What the law can do is to set out the parameters, the framework for the exercise of the powers and that is what we are doing.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Police will assess the nature of the crime, the evidence and whether to collect DNA information even if the offence is registrable or eligible.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Mr Pritam Singh's fourth question was to ask for the cost of taking a DNA sample.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is not possible to ascertain the cost of every individual isolated act.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: With that, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The first area is in respect of her reply to my query in my speech about whether or not a person would be warned of the consequences of not giving a blood sample to extract DNA information.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Minister of State mentioned that the current practice would be followed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, my question to her is whether the current practice is be updated to specifically mention about this new offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Minister of State mentioned that there are already provisions in these acts, meaning the MDA and the CLTPA, and therefore there is no need for consolidation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: My question is – what are the legislative safeguards for collection under the MDA and the CLTPA?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In principle, I do not see a difference between a convicted criminal and a ISA detainee, which is covered by the current Bill, and a drug addict of a Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act detainee.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For all of them, their DNA information should be safeguards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I seek the clarification from the learned Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: At the very least, can she perhaps assure the House that this will be looked at at some point in the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: I was not sure if I caught it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: How will the Police actually help those who are above 16 years old with disabilities, special needs or who do not have full mental capacity in, for example, the process of collecting blood samples and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: So, I just wanted to have some clarification on that.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: If you are not ready, it is okay, but please look into it and please just look into these two groups, especially.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: On the second question, I understand where the Member is coming from.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: We have tried to make the process as straightforward and as simple as possible.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They only need to fill up an online form, fill in the case number and as such.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: That is as simplified as we can make.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But I understand where the Member is coming from, that anything that is online may make it difficult for certain groups of individuals.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: But if there is difficulty that they face, they can raise it with us and we will see how to help them apply for their information to be removed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: When the law enforcement agency is getting consent from the person they are drawing the DNA sample from – it could be a suspect, it could be a volunteer – and that person is not comfortable in English, are there steps to make an interpreter present?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: So, I think for the situation that she shared, I believe the Police will be able to explain the process in the vernacular language that the accused person is comfortable with so that the suspect is able to comprehend and understand what is necessary from him or her.      .
